speaker: April Dunford
title: How to nail your product positioning | April Dunford (Obviously Awesome)
question: In B2B software, how can you tell when weak product positioning is the root problem?
guest: People ask me this a lot, and what I wish we had was a metric where you could say, when you start seeing this metric move, you know the positioning is bad. Unfortunately, weak positioning gets you all the way across the pipeline. It hurts you early because people don't get what you are, so they don't respond to marketing. You get sluggishness in the middle where the light doesn't come on until three calls with a sales rep. Sometimes sales is great at closing, so you win deals, and then customers use the product, realize it isn't what they expected, and churn out. So all your metrics look bad, making it really hard to measure. You can really hear it in initial sales calls. The most common sign is confusion, where the customer says, "Could you back up and pitch that from the beginning?" Even worse, they think they know what you are, but you aren't that—like saying, "I get it, you're just like Salesforce," when you're nothing like Salesforce. Or they say, "I totally get what you do, I just don't get why anyone would pay for that when I can do it in a spreadsheet."

points.core: No single funnel metric reliably isolates a product positioning problem.
points.note: Accept: weak positioning degrades metrics across every pipeline stage—marketing response, sales velocity, and post-sale churn—making dashboards inconclusive. Do not credit: generic advice to track conversion rates or run A/B tests.

points.core: Prospects repeatedly asking sales reps to restart the pitch signals confusion.
points.note: Accept: buyers saying 'back up and explain that again' or showing blank confusion on initial sales calls. Do not credit: vague mentions of poor messaging without describing prospect confusion in live calls.

points.core: Prospects equating the product to an unrelated incumbent signals category misclassification.
points.note: Accept: buyers saying 'you are just like [wrong competitor]' and forcing reps to correct the wrong mental model. Do not credit: generic remarks about competitive differentiation.

points.core: Prospects questioning why anyone would pay over a spreadsheet signals missing value.
points.note: Accept: buyers grasping what the product does but seeing no reason to pay for it over status-quo tools like spreadsheets. Do not credit: generic claims that pricing is too high.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Weak positioning is usually the root problem when the symptoms show up everywhere at once rather than in one funnel stage, and when fixing execution doesn't fix them.

The clearest signs come from prospects. They take most of a first call to grasp what you do, or they compare you to products you don't consider competitors. They say "this is cool" but can't say why they would buy it now. Many deals end in "no decision" rather than in a loss to a rival.

Internal signs matter too. Ask five people in sales, marketing and product who the product is for and why it wins; if you get five different answers, positioning is the gap. Other signs are sales reps each writing their own pitch, marketing messages that keep changing without improving conversion, and discounting to close deals because buyers don't see differentiated value.

The telling contrast is your best customers. If they love the product, renew and expand, yet new prospects don't get it, the product is fine and the framing is wrong. If even happy customers are rare, the problem is more likely the product or the market itself.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Weak positioning reveals itself through a telltale gap: existing best-fit customers love and retain your software—proving the product delivers real value—yet new prospects struggle to grasp what it actually does or why it matters. On sales calls, buyers stay confused until they see a lengthy demo, anchor you to the wrong market category, and compare you against irrelevant competitors, generating feature requests that pull your roadmap off course. Marketing campaigns may drive initial traffic, but deals stall mid-pipeline and face heavy price pressure because prospects view you as an interchangeable commodity rather than the obvious choice for an urgent problem. Internally, sales reps improvise their own pitches just to make the story land, while product, marketing, and leadership describe your ideal customer and differentiated value in conflicting ways. Meanwhile, poor-fit accounts still close on mismatched expectations, creating onboarding friction and early churn. When strong retention among core users coexists with chronic prospect confusion, wrong-category comparisons, and internal narrative drift, weak positioning—not product quality or channel execution—is the root problem.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Weak positioning usually shows up as problems spread across several teams that don't improve when you fix execution. Look for these signs:

- **Confused prospects.** Early calls get spent explaining what the product is. Buyers file you in the wrong category or compare you to the wrong competitors.
- **Losing to inaction.** Deals stall or go to "do nothing" rather than to a rival, because buyers can't see why the problem is urgent or why you're the answer.
- **Price pressure.** You discount heavily because the value isn't clear.
- **Inconsistent messaging.** Each rep tells a different story, the website differs from the sales deck, and good leads turn into poor-fit opportunities.

The best test is to compare your happiest customers with your pipeline. If retained customers get strong value but describe it differently than your marketing does, and new deals still struggle, the product works and the framing is wrong. If customers churn or rarely use the product, the problem is product-market fit, not positioning. Also, if new reps, campaigns or pricing changes don't help, the cause is probably upstream.

April Dunford's *Obviously Awesome* offers a practical way to diagnose and rebuild positioning.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Weak product positioning usually reveals itself when customers who understand the product love it, yet the broader market struggles to grasp what it is or why it matters. A classic tell is that prospects routinely compare you to the wrong alternatives—cheaper point solutions, legacy tools, or adjacent categories—forcing sales reps to spend the first half of every call correcting misconceptions. You also see deals stall in "no decision," because even interested champions cannot clearly articulate your distinct value to internal stakeholders. Another signal is a disconnect between marketing and reality: campaigns generate demos, but conversion collapses once prospects see the product, or your best customers describe your value differently than your homepage does. Internally, reps improvise conflicting pitches and the roadmap lacks focus. When retention is strong among a specific customer subset, yet winning new deals feels inexplicably hard, positioning—not the product or sales execution—is usually the root problem.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Weak positioning is likely the root problem when buyers who would benefit from your product consistently misunderstand what it does, who it’s for, or why they’d choose it over what they use today. You’ll hear the same confusion across sales calls and lost deals. Prospects compare you with tools built for a different job, ask for features they don’t need, or only see the value after a tailored demo. Meanwhile, customers who use the product for its strongest use case get clear value and stick around.

To test it, keep the product, price, and sales process steady. With comparable prospects, try a pitch that names the best-fit buyer, the problem they need to solve, and why your product beats their usual alternative. If buyers can explain the value back to you and more qualified deals advance, positioning was likely a bottleneck. If buyers understand the value and still stall over the same missing capability, implementation burden, or cost, investigate that obstacle.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Weak positioning is likely when the right customers get clear value after adopting the software, yet similar prospects struggle to explain who it’s for, why they need it, or why they’d choose it over what they use today. A telling sign is that deals move forward only after an experienced salesperson reframes the product. A low win rate alone tells you little.

To test the diagnosis, ask recent buyers what triggered their search, what they would have done without your product, and what made it worth switching. Use their answers to frame the product for comparable prospects while keeping the offer and sales process steady. If those prospects can explain the difference in their own words and more of them take a concrete next step, positioning was likely a bottleneck. If they already understand the value but consistently walk away over a missing capability, price, or low urgency, investigate that constraint first.
